subject: Coffee & Tea
title: The Coffee Belt
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Coffee Belt.

hook.text: All coffee grows between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn—a band called the Coffee Belt.

buildup.text: Around 70 countries in this belt grow coffee. Brazil, Vietnam, Colombia, Indonesia, and Ethiopia lead output.

discovery.text: Brazil alone produces a third of all coffee on Earth. A frost there can send global prices soaring overnight.

twist.text: Most Coffee Belt nations are developing economies. Their entire stability can hinge on one annual crop.

climax.text: Climate change is shrinking the Belt. Areas that grew coffee for centuries are becoming too warm.

punchline.text: A narrow tropical band feeds the world's caffeine addiction.

quiz.question: Which country produces about one-third of all coffee globally?

details.summary: The coffee belt spans the tropics between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, where conditions suit coffee cultivation. Over 70 countries grow coffee within this band, but the top five producers, Brazil, Vietnam, Colombia, Indonesia, and Ethiopia, account for most of global output.
details.whyItMatters: Geography concentrates coffee production in developing tropical nations, creating economic dependence and vulnerability to climate change across the entire belt.
takeaways: The coffee belt lies between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn
Five countries produce the majority of the world's coffee

faq.question: Which countries produce the most coffee?
faq.answer: Brazil leads by a wide margin at roughly 35 percent of global production. Vietnam is second at about 15 percent, followed by Colombia, Indonesia, and Ethiopia. Together these five countries produce over 70 percent of the world's coffee.

faq.question: Can coffee be grown outside the coffee belt?
faq.answer: Coffee requires consistent warmth and is frost-sensitive, essentially confining production to the tropics. Small experimental farms exist in California, Australia, and Japan, but commercial-scale production outside the belt is not economically viable.
